author: Tertullian
addressee: Christians troubled by heretical teachings about Christ's body
occasion: Tertullian writes to refute Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus, and others who denied that Christ had a true human body born from the Virgin Mary, because their denials undermine the Christian hope of the resurrection of the flesh.
argument: Tertullian argues that Christ truly took human flesh, born from the Virgin Mary, because only a body that is really born and really flesh can die and rise, and Christ's resurrection is the pledge of our own bodily resurrection. He first defends the fittingness of the incarnation against Marcion's claim that birth and flesh are unworthy of God. He then refutes alternative views: that Christ's flesh was sidereal, animal, spiritual, or angelic, showing from Scripture and reason that it was ordinary human flesh from Mary's womb. Finally he insists that this flesh was not sinful, though it was of the same nature as ours, and that its resurrection guarantees the resurrection of our flesh.

outline.move: Tertullian states the question: whether Christ had true human flesh, since this determines the resurrection of the flesh.
He confronts Marcion for rejecting the nativity and all its witnesses, and appeals to the rule of faith handed down from the apostles.
He argues that birth was not impossible or dangerous for God, since angels also truly appeared in human bodies.
He answers the objection that birth and flesh are shameful, showing that Christ loved the very human condition he came to redeem.
He argues that if Christ's flesh was unreal, his suffering, death, and resurrection were unreal, and Christian faith is empty.
He refutes Apelles' view that Christ had a real body not born but made of sidereal substance, by contrasting Christ's mission with that of angels.
He explains Christ's words 'Who is my mother and who are my brothers?' as a rebuke of unbelief, not a denial of his birth.
He argues against the Apelleans that if the world is sinful, sidereal flesh would be no purer than earthly flesh.
He shows that Christ's body displayed all the marks of earthly human flesh, including hunger, thirst, tears, fear, and blood.
He refutes the view that Christ's flesh was animate or made of soul-substance, showing that Christ came to save our non-carnal souls.
He argues that God did not need to make the soul visible by turning it into flesh; Christ showed a human soul by clothing it in flesh, not by making it flesh.
He argues that the soul already knows itself, so Christ came to reveal salvation, not the soul's nature.
He argues from the distinct names and Christ's own separate references to his soul and flesh that they are two substances, not one converted into the other.
He refutes the claim that Christ bore an angel, showing that Christ came as man to save man, and as God's own Son.
He refutes Valentinus' 'spiritual flesh' by citing prophets and apostles who call Christ a true man.
He clarifies that Christ took the likeness of sinful flesh, not sinful flesh itself, and that his flesh was of Adam's nature but without sin.
He explains why Christ had to be born of a virgin: to inaugurate a new birth and reverse the fall brought through Eve.
He argues that Christ, being God's Son by the Spirit, took his flesh from Mary without a human father.
He argues that John 1:13 refers to Christ's unique birth, against a heretical textual corruption that reads it as the spiritual seed of the elect.
He proves from Matthew, Paul, and the Psalms that Christ was born 'from' the Virgin, not merely 'through' her.
He argues from Isaiah's prophecy and Elizabeth's greeting that Mary truly conceived and bore Christ from her own flesh.
He shows from the genealogies and Paul that Christ's flesh descended from Abraham and David through Mary.
He defends the reality of Mary's childbearing against those who say she both did and did not give birth.
He shows that Scripture's plain names for flesh and Christ strike down all who divide or spiritualize his body.
He concludes that Christ's flesh was truly human and born of the Virgin, establishing the ground for defending our own resurrection.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Son of God, truly God and truly man, born of the Virgin Mary.

cast.name: Mary
cast.who: The Virgin Mother of Christ, from whose flesh he was born.

cast.name: Marcion
cast.who: Heretic who denied that Christ had true flesh or was truly born.

cast.name: Apelles
cast.who: Former disciple of Marcion who taught that Christ had a real body not born but made of sidereal substance.

cast.name: Valentinus
cast.who: Heretic who taught that Christ's flesh was spiritual.

cast.name: Philumene
cast.who: Virgin prophetess associated with Apelles, through whom he claimed angelic revelation.

cast.name: Alexander
cast.who: Heretic who misrepresented Tertullian's view as saying Christ's flesh was sinful.

cast.name: Ebion
cast.who: Heretic who taught that Jesus was a mere man from David's seed, not the Son of God.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: Patriarch from whose seed Christ descended according to the flesh.

cast.name: David
cast.who: King from whose seed Christ descended according to the flesh.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first man, whose flesh Christ took to redeem.

cast.name: Eve
cast.who: The first woman, whose fall through the serpent was reversed by Mary's faith.

cast.name: Gabriel
cast.who: The angel who announced Christ's conception to Mary.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: Prophet who foretold the Virgin birth.

cast.name: Jeremiah
cast.who: Prophet who spoke of the man Christ.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.who: Prophet who saw the Son of Man on the clouds.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: Apostle who taught Christ's true humanity and resurrection.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: Apostle who preached Jesus as a man sent by God.

cast.name: Matthew
cast.who: Evangelist who recorded Christ's genealogy from Abraham and David.

cast.name: John
cast.who: Evangelist who taught that the Word became flesh.

cast.name: Simeon
cast.who: Aged prophet who recognized the infant Christ as a sign to be contradicted.

cast.name: Elizabeth
cast.who: Mother of John the Baptist, who called Mary the mother of her Lord.

cast.name: Joseph
cast.who: Husband of Mary, of the line of David.

cast.name: Lazarus
cast.who: Man raised by Christ, whose flesh was ordinary human flesh.

cast.name: Solomon
cast.who: King of Israel, mentioned alongside Jonah as an example of a mere human son, to show that if Christ were only son of man and not also Son of God, he would have nothing more than Solomon or Jonah had.

cast.name: Jonah
cast.who: Prophet, mentioned alongside Solomon as an example of a mere human son, to show that if Christ were only son of man and not also Son of God, he would have nothing more than Solomon or Jonah had.

cast.name: Zechariah
cast.who: Prophet in whom an angel spoke, contrasted with Christ who spoke by his own authority.

cast.name: Ezekiel
cast.who: Prophet who spoke of a cow that calved and did not calve.

cast.name: Jesse
cast.who: Father of David, from whose root Christ as flower sprang.

key_terms.sense: Flesh, the material human body, especially Christ's true human body
Birth, especially Christ's true birth from the Virgin Mary
The Virgin Mary, and her virginal conception and childbearing
An unreal appearance or illusion, the heretical view of Christ's body
The resurrection of the dead, especially of the flesh, grounded in Christ's resurrection
The underlying reality or nature of a thing, especially of Christ's flesh
Spiritual, as opposed to fleshly; the heretical view of Christ's flesh
Soul-like or made of soul; the heretical view that Christ's flesh was soul
Made of stars or heavenly substance; Apelles' view of Christ's flesh
Sin, especially the sin of the flesh which Christ came to destroy
Man, human being; Christ as true man
Son of Man, Christ's title indicating his true humanity
Son of God, Christ's divine title
Seed, especially human seed from which Christ was not born, and the seed of David from which he was
Womb, especially Mary's womb from which Christ took flesh
The Word, God the Son, who became flesh

scripture: Tertullian uses the Septuagint/Vulgate book names and Psalm numbering. He cites Isaiah as Esaias, Jeremiah as Hieremias, Ezekiel as Ezechiel, and Zechariah as Zacharias. Psalms are cited by their Septuagint numbering, which is generally one behind the Hebrew numbering for Psalms 10–148; modern citations should use the Hebrew numbering with a note where the LXX numbering differs. He refers to the first man as Adam and to the books of the Acts of the Apostles as Acta Apostolorum.
uncertain: The exact date of composition; it is placed in Tertullian's Catholic period, likely c. 206–212, but cannot be fixed more precisely.
Whether the addressee is a specific individual or a general Christian readership; the text addresses heretics directly but is written for orthodox believers.
The precise identity of 'Alexander' in section 16; he is otherwise unknown and may be a local opponent.
The exact wording of some scriptural citations, which Tertullian may quote from memory or from an Old Latin version differing from modern critical texts.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Solomon... mentioned alongside Jonah as an example of a mere human son, to show that if Christ were only son of man and not also Son of God, he would have nothing more than Solomon or Jonah had.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Nunc ut simplicius respondeamus, non competebat ex semine humano dei filium nasci, ne, si totus esset filius hominis, non esset et dei filius, nihilque haberet amplius Salomone, et amplius Iona; aut de Hebionis opinione credendus erat.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Solomon and Jonah are mentioned as examples showing that if Christ were only son of man and not also Son of God, he would have nothing more than Solomon or Jonah had; but the point is specifically that he would be no more than Solomon or Jonah, not that Solomon and Jonah are 'mere human sons' used as negative examples—rather, they are positive examples of what Christ would merely be if he were not also Son of God.

Christ is quoted from Scripture in sections 5, 7, 13, 18, 24, but section 15 does not contain a direct quotation of Christ from Scripture. Section 15 contains prophetic and apostolic citations about Christ (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Paul, Peter), not Christ's own words.

Paul is quoted from Scripture in sections 16, 22, but section 20 does not contain a quotation of Paul. Section 20 cites Matthew ('Misit, inquit, deus filium suum factum ex muliere') and David/Psalms, not Paul.

Isaiah is quoted from Scripture in sections 14, 17, 21, 23, 24, but in section 14 the citation 'Non angelus neque legatus, sed ipse dominus salvos eos fecit' is from Isaiah 63:9, so this is correct. However, section 14's main Isaiah quotation is correct; no change needed for 14. The list is actually correct upon re-checking.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['15'], move: 'He refutes Valentinus' 'spiritual flesh' by citing prophets and apostles who call Christ a true man.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Licuit et Valentino ex privilegio haeretico carnem Christi spiritalem comminisci... Haec sola sufficere vice praescriptionis debuerunt ad testimonium carnis humanae et ex homine sumptae et non spiritalis, sicut nec animalis nec sidereae nec imaginariae, si sine studio et artifieio contentionis haereses esse potuissent.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 15 refutes Valentinus' 'spiritual flesh' not only by citing prophets and apostles, but primarily by arguing that if Christ's flesh were not human, he could not truly be called 'man' and 'Son of Man' as Scripture calls him. The section also includes a detailed critique of Valentinian reasoning about why Christ's flesh should not be earthly, and ends with a comparison of Valentinians to pagans/ethnici.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['19'], move: 'He argues that John 1:13 refers to Christ's unique birth, against a heretical textual corruption that reads it as the spiritual seed of the elect.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Sic enim scriptum esse contendunt: Nem ex sanguine nec ex carnis voluntate nec ex viri, sed ex deo nati sunt, quasi supra dictos credentes in nomine eius designet, ut ostendat esse semen illud arcanum electorum et spiritalium, quod sibi imbuunt.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 19 argues that John 1:13 refers to Christ's unique birth, against a heretical reading that applies it to believers as the spiritual seed of the elect. However, Tertullian does not describe this as a 'textual corruption' (though it may be); he says 'Sic enim scriptum esse contendunt'—'for so they contend it is written'—presenting it as the heretics' interpretation of the text, not necessarily a different textual reading.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Lazarus... Man raised by Christ, whose flesh was ordinary human flesh.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Lazarus is mentioned in section 9 ('lacrimatus est super Lazarum') and section 12 ('Sed et hoc non aliter in se quam in Lazaro aliquo, cuius caro non erat animalis, ita nec anima carnalis'), but only as an example of resurrection, not as someone whose 'flesh was ordinary human flesh' in a way that contributes to the argument. The brief's description overstates his role; he is not a significant 'cast' member but a passing example.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Zechariah... Prophet in whom an angel spoke, contrasted with Christ who spoke by his own authority.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Nisi quod a Christo nunquam est dictum: Et ait mihi angelus, qui in me loquebatur. Sed nec quotidianum illud omnium prophetarum: Haec dicit dominus. Ipse enim erat dominus coram ex sua auctoritate pronuntians: Ego autem dico vobis.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Zechariah is mentioned in section 14, but the contrast is not that 'an angel spoke in him' versus Christ's own authority. Rather, Tertullian says Christ never said 'And the angel said to me, who spoke in me' (a phrase from Zechariah), nor did he use the prophets' formula 'Thus says the Lord,' because he himself was the Lord speaking with his own authority. The brief's description is slightly inaccurate: Zechariah is mentioned as an example of prophetic formula, not as someone 'in whom an angel spoke' in contrast to Christ.
